findings.element: .b-dayWrap / .b-dayCount / .b-dayRule — the wedding morning, the only centred type in the lab
findings.problem: Driven at 390, 768, 1280 and 1440 I read text-align on every composed surface: .b-field is start, .b-print is start, .b-ended is start, .b-og is start. Exactly one block in the whole lab is centred — .b-dayWrap — and it is on the screen the company gets judged by. Worse, the centring stops four lines in: MARA & FINN, "Today" at 96px, "Saturday 3 October 2026" and "This is the day the plan was for." are symmetric, and then HAPPENING NOW, "Wedding day at The Orchard", HOW YOU GOT HERE and KEPT BY ORLA all snap back to a hard left rag, with a centred 200px indigo rule sitting above full-bleed hairlines. The reader gets two documents stapled together on a 346px measure. The argument for a ceremonial register is real, but the thesis of this direction is a vertical measure — a left-hand spine on which a pixel is a unit of time — and the morning is the day that spine was built for, so it is the one screen that must not walk away from it. The centring also breaks the count's own alignment: the 96px T starts 48px in from the field edge, where the 96px 79 on the horizon hangs on the margin. And the optical correction written for exactly that, margin-left: -0.02em on .b-dayCount, computes to 0px at every width — the margin: 0 0 16px shorthand three declarations later resets it — so the correction that was written is not on the page.
findings.fix: In b.css set .b-dayWrap { text-align: start; } and .b-dayRule { margin: 0 0 24px; width: 100%; } so the accent rule becomes the full-width divider its neighbours already are. In .b-dayCount delete the dead margin-left: -0.02em line and write the shorthand as margin: 0 0 16px -0.02em; so the correction survives. Then assert in interaction-check.mjs, at 390/768/1280/1440 on state=day, that the left edge of the first glyph of .b-dayCount is within 1px of the left edge of .b-who, and that no element inside .b-field computes a text-align other than start.

findings.element: .b-behindRow — the cancelled record row ("City hotel shortlist" / "Not going ahead")
findings.problem: Measured on state=day, phone, desk, print and owner-flight at 390/768/1280/1440: the title lane renders 94.6-96.6px wide and 45px tall — two lines, with the single word "shortlist" alone on the second — while .b-behindState renders 125.4px on one line. The row reserves 96px for a .b-behindDate that is empty on this row (measured width 96, height 0), then two 14px gaps, then hands the 11px mono status label 125.4px via margin-left:auto, leaving the couple's own words 97px of a 346px row. The machine's annotation is 29 percent wider than the person's words, and the person's words are the only thing on the row that breaks. It is the one line item on the wedding morning carrying a human sentence, and it is the item the layout squeezes. It holds at every width because the day and phone media stay 388px whatever the window does, so no width in the set escapes it.
findings.fix: In b.css add .b-behindDate:empty { display: none; } so a dateless row stops paying 110px for an absent lane, and add .b-behindTitle { min-width: 0; }. Then make the state label yield rather than the title: change .b-behindRow to display: grid; grid-template-columns: 96px minmax(0, 1fr); column-gap: 14px; row-gap: 2px; align-items: baseline; with .b-behindState { grid-column: 2; justify-self: start; margin: 0; } so wherever both are present the label sits on its own line under the title in the label register. Assert in interaction-check.mjs that no .b-behindTitle renders narrower than the .b-behindState in its own row, and that no .b-behindTitle renders more than one line, at 390/768/1280/1440 across day, phone, desk, print and owner-flight.

findings.element: .b-og, .b-ogWho, .b-ogNum, .b-ogDate — the card as it lands in a chat
findings.problem: The card declares aspect-ratio: 1200/630 and then sets every value in absolute pixels: padding 18px, .b-ogWho 12px, .b-ogNum 64px, .b-ogDate 15px. Driven at every width the box measures 298 x 156.4, so the specimen is a picture of the shipped asset at 24.8 percent — but the type is not. The real Open Graph image is composed at 1200 x 630, where those same rules put the count at 64px on a 1200px card: 5.3 percent of the card width against the 21.5 percent the specimen shows, a factor of four. Nothing in the lab expresses the card's type as a proportion of the card, so the one guest-facing artifact whose entire job is to be legible at an unknown render size has been specified only at a size it will never actually be rendered at. This is the surface every guest passes through first and no seat has spent a pass on it.
findings.fix: Give the card its own container and set its type in container units so one rule set composes both renders. In b.css: .b-og { container-type: inline-size; padding: 6cqw; }, .b-ogWho { font-size: 4.03cqw; }, .b-ogNum { font-size: 21.48cqw; }, .b-ogDate { font-size: 5.03cqw; } — keeping each current px value as the preceding declaration so a browser without cqw falls back to today's rendering. Tracking is already in em and scales for free. Then add a second render in the harness at 1200 x 630 and assert every type box in the 1200px render is within 1 percent of 4.03x its box in the 298px render.

findings.problem: The leading ladder landed and the gate now enforces membership, which is why every ratio on the page is one of the six. It does not enforce the binding, and the binding is where the drift went. Measured across 11 states and 4 widths, one identical setting — 11px Geist Mono, uppercase, 1.76px tracking — renders at three leadings: 1.2 on .b-origin (20 instances), 1.4 on .b-behindDate, .b-behindLabel, .b-behindState, .b-behindCount, .b-label, .b-measureHead, .b-todayLabel and .b-unit (228 instances), and 1.5 on .b-date, .b-where, .b-inert and .b-grabWord (220 instances). A near-even split is drift, not a role split, and shell.css documents --lead-label as exactly this role. The same failure runs through the two most repeated objects: the moment title is --lead-date (1.3) as .b-title and --lead-head (1.2) as .b-dayNowTitle at the same 24px/600 on the day screen, and the ceremonial date line is --lead-date (1.3) as .b-when and --lead-label (1.4) as .b-dayDate at the same 20px/400. The gate cannot see any of it because every value is legal; only driving both screens shows the same object standing on two baselines, which is the precise defect shell.css says the ladder was declared to end.
findings.fix: Bind by role in b.css: set .b-date, .b-where, .b-inert, .b-grabWord and .b-origin to line-height: var(--lead-label); set .b-title to line-height: var(--lead-head); set .b-dayDate and .b-ogDate to line-height: var(--lead-date). Then extend audit.mjs from membership to binding with three assertions read off the rendered page: every element computing 11px Geist Mono with text-transform uppercase resolves to 1.4; every moment title (.b-title, .b-dayNowTitle) resolves to 1.2 on every medium; every ceremonial date line (.b-when, .b-dayDate, .b-ogDate) resolves to 1.3.

findings.element: .b-skel — the four bars in the loading frame (render-b.js lines 1192-1195)
findings.problem: All four skeleton bars are width:100%, so they render 346px wide against real content of 90px (the couple's name), 107px (the count), 236px ("Saturday 3 October 2026") and 208px ("Wedding day at The Orchard"). The frame promises four full-bleed headlines and delivers a short name, a two-digit numeral and two ranged-left lines, so roughly 70 percent of the reserved ink evaporates in front of the reader. The vertical reserve is wrong too: measured against state=phone at 390, .b-sub lands at y=191 but its bar sits at y=198, and the hairline and "Today is 16 July" below inherit the same 7px, so the whole lower half of the screen hops up the instant data arrives — the count bar is 83px where the count is 86px, and the gap under the date bar is 10px where the real gap is 4px. Below the hairline the loading frame reserves nothing at all, while eight moment rows are about to fill the rest of the screen.
findings.fix: In render-b.js size each bar to the box it stands in for: bar 1 width:96px;height:17px;margin-bottom:22px, bar 2 width:112px;height:86px;margin-bottom:10px, bar 3 width:236px;height:26px;margin-bottom:4px, bar 4 width:208px;height:23px. Add exactly one moment-row reserve below the hairline at the real .b-item geometry (a 76px x 15px date bar beside a 236px x 22px title bar, 42px tall, one row and never two). Then assert in interaction-check.mjs that every .b-skel box is within 2px of the box the loaded state renders in the same slot, at 390/768/1280/1440.

biggestWin: The tracking ladder is no longer a claim in a stylesheet, it is a measurable property of the page: driven across 11 states and 4 widths, every rendered size inside the artifact resolves to its declared step with no exceptions, the 96px word on the wedding morning is now set in the reading face rather than the code face, every date binds its parts with real non-breaking spaces, and figures are tabular everywhere they can change. Two weights, one family and six tracking steps are carrying a hierarchy most products need four weights and a second family to reach, and the A4 keepsake comes out of the same system without a parallel stylesheet. That is Vercel-Geist-grade discipline, and everything still wrong is a binding or a reserve problem sitting on top of a system that is right.
